clue.text: Native poet’s back in Italy more than once

definitions.note: Native stands for a native of Israel; the clue leans on the rest of the sentence to supply the country

indicators.note: the poet's name is read back to front
the turned name sits inside the two Is

blocks.note: I is the international code for Italy; the first of two
LEAR'S, the nonsense poet Edward Lear's, turned round
Italy used a second time, I again

explanation.surface: A native poet seems to keep going back to Italy, visit after visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More than once' tells you to use Italy's I twice, one on each side. Edward Lear is the crossword's favourite poet; his name with its 's turns into SRAEL.
explanation.definitionFit: An Israeli is a native of Israel, though 'native' alone is a thin definition, as solvers on the day remarked.

clue.text: Correspondence of form is second rising art movement

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading upwards, so MO turns round

blocks.note: MO, a second or moment, written upwards
Orphism, the colourful abstract style of Robert Delaunay

explanation.surface: A critic notes that a rising art movement shares its form with another.
explanation.walkthrough: Orphism is an obscure offshoot of Cubism, so the last seven letters may need the definition first. 'Second' is MO, as in 'wait a mo'.
explanation.definitionFit: Isomorphism is identity or close similarity of form, in crystals, organisms or mathematical structures.

clue.text: Magistrate is concerned with always finishing early

indicators.note: the word stops one letter before its end

blocks.note: re = concerning, as in a memo heading

explanation.surface: A magistrate who is forever leaving work before time.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a lazy official, but 'finishing early' is an instruction to cut the last letter of EVER.
explanation.definitionFit: A reeve was a local magistrate or chief officer of a town or district in Anglo-Saxon England.

clue.text: Startling beat captured by revolutionary recording

indicators.note: the beat is held inside the recording
a revolution turns the word round

blocks.note: TAPE reversed to EPAT, opening round the beat
to tan someone's hide is to beat them
the closing letter of the reversed tape

explanation.surface: A startling beat is captured on some revolutionary recording.
explanation.walkthrough: Épatant is French borrowed into English, as in épater les bourgeois. 'Beat' reads as a rhythm on the record, but it is the thrashing sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Épatant means shocking or startling, especially to conventional people.

clue.text: What led to the growth of cities badly invited rural solution

definitions.text: What led to the growth of cities

indicators.note: the letters are put together badly, so rearranged

explanation.surface: Planners invited a rural fix for sprawling cities, and it went badly.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder's own words, rural and solution, sit well with city growth, which helps hide that they are raw letters. Twenty letters make a long anagram, so crossing letters are worth getting first.
explanation.definitionFit: The Industrial Revolution drew workers from the land into factory towns, causing cities to grow fast.

clue.text: Guess your setter’s in the commons?

indicators.note: the setter's I'M goes inside

blocks.note: ESTATE: the commons are the third estate of the realm; it opens here
the rest of ESTATE closes round I'M

explanation.surface: A voter asks whether the crossword setter might be sitting in the House of Commons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your setter' is how a crossword compiler refers to themself, so it gives I or ME, here I'M. The three estates were clergy, nobles and commons.
explanation.definitionFit: To estimate is to make a rough guess at a value or amount.

clue.text: Try to hear birds during English fall

indicators.note: the birds come in the middle of the fall

blocks.note: Aves is the Latin name for the class of birds

explanation.surface: Birdwatchers straining to hear birds during an English autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall' is the American word for autumn in the surface, but it is a DROP here. AVES comes from biology, the class name for all birds.
explanation.definitionFit: To eavesdrop is to listen in secretly, trying to hear what others say.

clue.text: Go round one foreign city

indicators.note: the word for go goes round the one

blocks.note: TURN, a go or go on your turn; it opens here

explanation.surface: Advice to a tourist: go round a single foreign city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' reads as a verb, but it is the noun TURN, as in 'whose go is it?'.
explanation.definitionFit: Turin is a city in north-west Italy, so foreign to a British setter.

clue.text: Ten images repositioned to make attractive

indicators.note: the letters are put in new positions

explanation.surface: A designer moves ten pictures around a wall to make it look better.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as interior design, with 'attractive' meaning pretty; the answer takes it in the physical sense of pulling metal.
explanation.definitionFit: To magnetise something is to give it magnetic power, literally making it attractive.

clue.text: Time to go on social media site with new name

definitions.text: social media site with new name

blocks.note: to witter is to talk on and on about trivia

explanation.surface: Time to leave the social media site that has been renamed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go on' reads as 'continue'; here it means to chatter at length. Witter is chiefly British: to prattle pointlessly.
explanation.definitionFit: Twitter was renamed X in 2023, hence 'with new name'.

clue.text: Is correspondence for him?

definitions.note: the definition is a pronoun standing for a man's name

explanation.surface: Someone at the door asks whether the post is for a particular man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Him' is a bare pointer to some man's name, the clue's question mark admitting the looseness. Ismail is a common Muslim given name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ismail is a man's name, the Arabic form of Ishmael, so 'him' can point to him.

clue.text: Situation confused Bangladesh after boy goes missing

indicators.note: the remaining letters are mixed up
the boy's letters are taken out

explanation.surface: A news report: after a boy vanishes, Bangladesh is in confusion.
explanation.walkthrough: LAD is the crossword's usual boy. Take it out of Bangladesh and the seven letters left make SHEBANG.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebang is a situation or affair, as in 'the whole shebang'.

clue.text: One attacking a small southern tree of heaven endlessly

indicators.note: the tree's name loses its ending

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothes labels
AILANTHUS, the tree of heaven, with its ending HUS cut

explanation.surface: Someone attacks a small southern tree of heaven, and keeps on without end.
explanation.walkthrough: The tree of heaven is Ailanthus, a fast-growing Chinese tree common in cities. 'Endlessly' here cuts three letters, which is generous.
explanation.definitionFit: An assailant is one who attacks another.

clue.text: Tenant of fields and house with tree outside

indicators.note: the tree goes outside the house

blocks.note: ELDER, a tree; it opens here

explanation.surface: A tenant farmer rents fields and a house with a tree standing outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' reads as part of the tenant's description, but it only joins. LEA is a poetic meadow, a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A leaseholder holds a property on a lease, so is a tenant.

clue.text: Often finished a new port before answer’s found in a gin

indicators.note: the pieces so far come ahead of the next
the answer's A is placed inside A GIN

blocks.note: A GIN, opening round the answer
the closing letters of A GIN

explanation.surface: Someone often ended up at a new port, a gin in hand before the answer came.
explanation.walkthrough: A long charade in which each word does one small job. Dover is England's main Channel ferry port.
explanation.definitionFit: Over and over again means repeatedly, very often.

clue.text: Text from college is hardly one that’s entertaining

indicators.note: the answer is lifted from the words that follow

blocks.note: the answer runs from the end of college, through is, into the start of hardly

explanation.surface: A student notes that a college text is hardly entertaining reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardly one that's entertaining' reads as a sneer at the text; the definition is just 'one that's entertaining', and 'hardly' supplies HA.
explanation.definitionFit: A geisha is a Japanese woman trained to entertain guests with music, dance and conversation.

clue.text: Everything’s as it should be here in a large country, right?

indicators.note: the word for here sits inside the country

blocks.note: LAND, a country; it opens here
here, as in answering a roll call

explanation.surface: A proud citizen declares all is well in a big country, and asks for agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing 'right?' reads as a tag question but is the last chunk, CORRECT. The phrase is a military report that all personnel and kit are accounted for.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from military roll calls and kit inspections, now used of anything found in proper order.

clue.text: Sign of resistance returning a possible diamond ring

indicators.note: the pieces come back, read right to left

blocks.note: a diamond is one kind of gem

explanation.surface: A woman hands back a diamond ring as a sign she resists the proposal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a refused engagement, but 'resistance' is electrical: the ohm's symbol is the Greek capital omega, Ω.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega (Ω) is the symbol for the ohm, the unit of electrical resistance.

clue.text: Suspicion mostly to take possession of girl

indicators.note: most of the word is used: its last letter goes

blocks.note: sus, informal British for suspicion, as in 'on sus'
ANNEX, to take possession of, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A jealous suitor's suspicion leads him mostly to want to possess a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' sits between the two pieces and applies to the one after it. Sus is British slang for suspicion, source of the old 'sus law' on stop and search.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: Susanne is one of countless female given names, the kind of vague pointer only crossings pin down.

clue.text: Stag, elk, skate and civet all essentially are big-mouthed

indicators.note: the essence, or middle, of each of the four words

blocks.note: the middle two letters of sTAg
the middle three letters of sKATe
the middle three letters of cIVEt

explanation.surface: A naturalist claims that stags, elks, skates and civets all have big mouths.
explanation.walkthrough: The middles are of different lengths, one, two or three letters, which is what makes this hard to spot. 'Big-mouthed' reads as jaws on animals but means chatty.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone big-mouthed talks too much, so is talkative.

clue.text: Decorator is power finishing before beginning to repaint

indicators.note: the first letter of repaint

blocks.note: last, as in the finishing one
ere is old or poetic for before

explanation.surface: A decorator is energetically finishing the job before starting to repaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' reads as the order of work, but it is the word ERE. A plasterer's trade is close to a decorator's.
explanation.definitionFit: A plasterer finishes walls and ceilings and can be called a decorator, especially of ornamental plasterwork.

clue.text: Lack of vigour I intend getting raised in drinkers’ group

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means written upwards
the turned phrase goes inside the group

blocks.note: AA, Alcoholics Anonymous; it opens here
I MEAN, I intend, turned upwards

explanation.surface: A member of a drinkers' support group plans to raise their lack of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: The drinkers' group is AA, which ironically is for people who have stopped drinking. 'Getting' is part of the reversal instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Anaemia is a lack of red blood cells, and figuratively a lack of vigour or spirit.

clue.text: Bird’s cry caught greeting noise of cat returning

indicators.note: the cat's noise comes back, read right to left

explanation.surface: A bird's cry, caught when it greets a cat that has come back purring.
explanation.walkthrough: C for caught comes from cricket scorecards. The cat purring back into the scene becomes a reversed PURR.
explanation.definitionFit: A chirrup is a bird's short chirping cry.

clue.text: Boasted less than attractive hair style

indicators.note: the word falls short of its full length by a letter

blocks.note: crew is an old past tense of crow, to boast
CUTE, attractive, less its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone boasted about a hairstyle that was less than attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less than attractive' reads as mildly ugly, but it means CUTE short of a letter. CREW as a past tense of crow is now rare outside the cock that crew.
explanation.definitionFit: A crew cut is a very short, bristly hair style.

clue.text: Droppings round horse’s back absorbing upper-class

indicators.note: the horse word is read backwards
the turned word takes in U

blocks.note: NAG, a horse, turned to GAN; it opens here
U = upper-class, as in 'U and non-U' English

explanation.surface: Manure spread round a horse's rear, soaking up some posh stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse's back' reads as the animal's rear, but it is NAG read back. 'Round' leads the clue yet its O lands last.
explanation.definitionFit: Guano is the droppings of seabirds or bats, used as fertiliser.

clue.text: Sleep during sex is not appropriate

indicators.note: the sleep comes in the middle of sex

blocks.note: IT, crossword slang for sex; it opens here

explanation.surface: Nodding off in bed at the wrong moment is not appropriate.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex (or sex appeal) is an old slang use the crossword keeps alive.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the prefix IN- negates APT, just as NOT negates appropriate.

clue.text: One supporting swine with swine supporting them initially

indicators.note: what comes initially is what comes first, so only the first letter of them is used
in a down clue, the swine is written below T, holding it up

blocks.note: the second swine: a rotter, a nasty person; supporting puts it beneath T

explanation.surface: A riddle about pigs holding each other up.
explanation.walkthrough: The two swines differ: the first is a pig, whose feet support it; the second is a person, a rotter. In a down clue, supporting means placed underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A trotter is a pig's foot, which supports the animal.

clue.text: Arrest — surprisingly resistance happened

indicators.note: the letters come out in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: An arrest was made; surprisingly, there was resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a police report, and resistance fits an arrest so well that R is easy to miss as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from police language, where apprehending a suspect means seizing them.

clue.text: Fabric printer’s measure, one coming in 500 metres

indicators.note: the measure and the one go inside

blocks.note: D = 500 in Roman numerals; D M opens here
an en is a printer's unit of width
M = metres, closing round EN and I

explanation.surface: A printer measures out fabric, one piece arriving in a 500-metre roll.
explanation.walkthrough: '500 metres' looks like a length of cloth, but it splits into D (Roman 500) and M (metres). The printer's measures are EM and EN.
explanation.definitionFit: Denim is the tough cotton twill fabric used for jeans.

clue.text: Extremely happy former partner dealt with changes

indicators.note: the letters of dealt are changed around

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted that their ex has dealt with some changes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dealt with changes' reads as coping; 'with' only joins, and 'changes' tells you to shuffle DEALT.
explanation.definitionFit: Exalted can mean elated, in a state of extreme happiness.

clue.text: Champion keeping school solvent

indicators.note: the champion holds the school inside

blocks.note: ACE, a champion; it opens here
Eton College, the English public school

explanation.surface: A champion keeps her school financially solvent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solvent' reads as out of debt; it is the chemical sense. Eton is the crossword's default school.
explanation.definitionFit: Acetone is a common solvent, used in nail-varnish remover.

clue.text: Result of pressing investigation — shells perhaps covered in minute chickpeas?

indicators.note: the shells go inside the minute

blocks.note: shells are one kind of ammunition
gram is the Indian name for chickpeas

explanation.surface: A cook covers shells with tiny chickpeas after pressing them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressing' reads as urgent, but a mammogram is taken while the breast is pressed between plates. Gram is the chickpea in Indian cooking, as in gram flour.
explanation.definitionFit: A mammogram is the X-ray image from a breast examination done by compressing the breast.

clue.text: Silently contemplated sea engulfing you and me

indicators.note: the sea swallows you and me

blocks.note: MED, the Mediterranean; it opens here

explanation.surface: Staring quietly at a sea wave that might swallow the two of us.
explanation.walkthrough: The sea here is the Med, the common short form of the Mediterranean.
explanation.definitionFit: To muse is to think quietly and at length, so mused means silently contemplated.

clue.text: Spice island stripped fennec pelt

indicators.note: the fox's outer letters are stripped off

blocks.note: a cay is a low island or reef
to pepper is to pelt with shot or missiles

explanation.surface: An island trader sells spice and a fennec fox's stripped pelt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pelt' reads as a fur, which fits the fox, but it is the verb, to bombard. A fennec is a small big-eared desert fox.
explanation.definitionFit: Cayenne pepper is a hot spice made from ground chillies.

clue.text: Unknown typefaces including Roman capital can be pants

indicators.note: to include is to hold within, so the typefaces take R inside them

explanation.surface: A designer complains that unknown typefaces, even Roman capitals, can be pants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' in the surface is British slang for rubbish; in the answer it means underpants. 'Roman capital' reads as a typeface style but is the first letter of Roman.
explanation.definitionFit: Y-fronts are men's briefs with a Y-shaped front seam; in Britain, pants are underpants.

clue.text: Dog secured by lead — better late than never?

indicators.note: the dog is held inside the lead

blocks.note: PB, the chemical symbol for lead; it opens here
a stock name for a dog

explanation.surface: Putting a dog on its lead: better late than never.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' is a dog's leash in the surface but the metal Pb here. The definition is an example, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Better late than never' is a well-known proverb.

clue.text: Caller chasing good state nurse

indicators.note: the caller comes behind the good state

explanation.surface: A caller pursues a nurse employed by the good state.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a health visitor is a community nurse who visits families at home, especially those with babies. 'Chasing' puts VISITOR second.
explanation.definitionFit: A health visitor is a nurse who visits people in their homes.

clue.text: Manually produced pair of taps, judged about fine

indicators.note: the judged word goes round fine

blocks.note: H and C, the hot and cold taps

explanation.surface: A plumber's pair of hand-made taps was judged about fine.
explanation.walkthrough: The pair of taps is literally H AND C, the hot and cold labels, so the word AND comes free.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: manual comes from the Latin for hand, so manually produced is crafted by hand.

clue.text: What beats transport system old men reconstructed

indicators.note: the letters of old men are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: Old men rebuilt a transport system that beats anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What beats' reads as a boast; it means a device that ticks out beats. Old is O.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic-flavoured description: the device ticks out a steady pulse, so it is literally the thing that beats.

clue.text: Modern teen’s involved record of lawbreaking

indicators.note: the letters are tangled up

explanation.surface: A modern teenager is involved in some offence on their record.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain an endorsement is a note of a driving offence put on your licence, along with penalty points.
explanation.definitionFit: An endorsement on a driving licence records a traffic offence.

clue.text: One not taking sides, nervous about end of conflict

indicators.note: the nervous word goes round the letter
the last letter of conflict

blocks.note: NEURAL, of the nerves; it opens here

explanation.surface: A neutral country is nervous about how a conflict will end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nervous' reads as anxious; here it means to do with nerves, NEURAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A neutral is a person or state that takes no side in a conflict.

clue.text: Stubbs maybe finished — in the end had to keep roan’s head simple

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only the final D of had is used
the finished word holds roan's first letter
a head sits at the top, so roan's head is its first letter

explanation.surface: George Stubbs finished his painting of a roan horse in a simple style.
explanation.walkthrough: Stubbs and roan conjure George Stubbs, the horse painter, but the Stubbs meant is Una Stubbs, a British TV actress. 'Maybe' flags her as one example of a Stubbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Unadorned means plain, without decoration, so simple.

clue.text: Party dress to discard, one going with black attire

blocks.note: to can something is to scrap it

explanation.surface: Advice to throw out a party frock and go in black instead.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dominicans are the Black Friars, named for their black cloaks; London's Blackfriars is named after them.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dominican friar wears a black mantle over a white habit.

clue.text: French writer meaning to get translated

indicators.note: the letters are carried over into a new form

explanation.surface: A French writer whose meaning is to be translated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Translated' fits a French writer perfectly, which hides that it is only shuffling the letters of 'meaning to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Michel de Montaigne was the sixteenth-century French essayist.

clue.text: What helps people get on university course

blocks.note: the rapport between people who click

explanation.surface: Something that helps students get ahead at university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get on' reads as succeed, but it means get along with each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Chemistry is both the attraction between people and a science taught at university.

clue.text: Make improvements to staff editor retains

indicators.note: the editor keeps the staff inside

blocks.note: ED, an editor, opening round the staff

explanation.surface: An editor keeps on the staff, making improvements to them.
explanation.walkthrough: Staff here is people, MEN, not a stick. The editor is the usual ED.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym used of texts: editors emend a manuscript by correcting it.

clue.text: Pandemonium as Charles embraces Oscar

indicators.note: Charles wraps round Oscar

blocks.note: CHAS, short for Charles, opening round Oscar

explanation.surface: Uproar breaks out when Charles hugs an Oscar winner.
explanation.walkthrough: Chas is the written short form of Charles. Oscar is O in the radio alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: Milton coined Pandemonium as the capital of Hell, and the word now means wild uproar.

clue.text: Certain to limit tattoo’s size?

indicators.note: the certain word goes round the tattoo, hemming it in

explanation.surface: A tattooist is sure to keep a tattoo's size down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tat' is informal for a tattoo. The 's only joins it to the definition, which is 'size', with a question mark for the looseness.
explanation.definitionFit: Stature is a person's height, their bodily size.

clue.text: News — it is interrupted by Scottish strike

indicators.note: the strike breaks into 'tis

blocks.note: to ding is Scots for to strike

explanation.surface: A news flash: a Scottish strike has interrupted things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' suggests industrial action; here it is a blow, the Scots verb ding.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though tidings is the older, literary word, as in 'good tidings of great joy'.

clue.text: Look down on little sister holding on to papa in river

indicators.note: the sister holds papa inside
the whole lot sits in the river

blocks.note: DEE, a river; it opens here
SIS, short for sister; it opens round P

explanation.surface: A little sister clings to dad in the river, looking down on the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nest: P inside SIS, then SPIS inside DEE. The Dee is a river in Scotland and another on the Welsh border.

clue.text: Royal weapon of unknown calibre set in a lot of gems all over

indicators.note: most of the word: its last letter goes
the gems word is turned over, read backwards
the unknown and calibre are set inside

blocks.clueFragment: a lot of gems all over
blocks.note: RUBIE(S) reversed to EIBUR; it opens here

blocks.clueFragment: a lot of gems all over
blocks.note: EIBUR closes round X and CAL

explanation.surface: A royal weapon of unknown bore is set among a hoard of gems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calibre' fits a weapon so well it hides that it only gives the abbreviation CAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Excalibur is King Arthur's sword, a royal weapon.

clue.text: Burning smell around one type of battery?

indicators.note: the smell goes around the one

blocks.note: HUM, a bad smell; it opens here

explanation.surface: A burning smell comes from around a battery.
explanation.walkthrough: Hum is British slang for a bad smell. The surface of an overheating battery is apt for lithium cells.

clue.text: A god turned insect? Almost freakish

indicators.note: the god's name is turned round
the insect falls one letter short

explanation.surface: A god transformed into an insect: nearly bizarre enough to be myth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' sounds like a transformation, but it only reverses AMON. The question mark after 'insect' hides that 'Almost' begins a new instruction.

clue.text: Workshop I later rebuilt to conserve energy

indicators.note: the letters are built into a new order
the jumble keeps the E inside it

blocks.note: E = energy, kept inside the mix

explanation.surface: An owner says he later rebuilt his workshop to save energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conserve energy' reads as green building, but it tells you to hold E in the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An atelier is a workshop or studio, especially an artist's or designer's.

clue.text: Exclusive landed in middle of week

indicators.note: the landed word goes inside
the centre letters of week

blocks.note: the middle letters of wEEk, EE; it opens here
a bird lit on a branch

explanation.surface: An exclusive flight that landed in the middle of the week.

explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym used as an adjective, as in an elite club open only to a chosen few.

clue.text: Part of painting exhibiting slight colouration

the words put the answer on show

blocks.note: the answer straddles the gap: the end of painting and the start of exhibiting

explanation.surface: An art critic notes that part of a painting shows a faint tint.

clue.text: Elbow groom into picture — but there’s no room

what is left goes into the picture

GROOM minus ROOM, since there's no room

clue.text: Language feature associated with Oxford?

blocks.note: a language, as in the one you learn at your mother's knee

explanation.surface: A linguistic feature linked with Oxford, perhaps its accent.

clue.text: I note golf might be derived from this kids’ game?

definitions.text: I note golf might be derived from this kids’ game?

blocks.note: the surface: some sport grew out of a playground game
the meaning: the letter in the middle of the word PIGGY is G, which is golf in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A sports historian muses that golf might have grown out of a children's game.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer literally: what is in the middle of PIGGY? Its third letter, G, and G is golf in the radio alphabet. Piggy in the middle is a game where one child tries to intercept a ball thrown over them.
explanation.definitionFit: Piggy in the middle is a children's ball game, and literally the middle of PIGGY is G for golf.

clue.text: Avoid motorway in bumpy vehicle

explanation.surface: Advice to avoid the motorway when travelling in a bumpy old car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as travelling inside the vehicle, but it only joins. British motorways are numbered M1, M25 and so on. A dodgem is a bumper car.
explanation.definitionFit: A dodgem is a fairground bumper car, built for bumping.

clue.text: Consecrated ground church gauge the ultimate in holy

indicators.note: ultimate means last, so the ultimate in holy is its last letter

explanation.surface: A churchyard said to be the last word in holiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The ultimate in holy' reads as the height of sanctity, but it means its last letter. CE is the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: a burial ground is blessed, or consecrated, before the dead are laid in it.
